questions.stem: The muscle, the driving force of the locomotor system:
options: Can only be stimulated by a nervous excitation
Is studied by arthrology
Can be stimulated by electrical, thermal or painful excitation
Contracts (shortens) under the influence of a stimulus
Is studied by myology
questions.explanation: Stimuli can be nervous, electrical, thermal, painful, etc. Myology studies muscles; arthrology studies joints.

questions.stem: Which of the following are roles of muscles?
options: Maintaining posture
Visceral functions such as blood propulsion and childbirth
Heat production (thermogenesis)
Protection of the viscera
Storage of calcium
questions.explanation: Roles: movement, thermogenesis, posture, joint stabilization, protection of the viscera and visceral functions (digestion, urination, blood propulsion, vasomotricity, childbirth…). Calcium storage is not among them.

options: Is also called striped or red muscle
Is made of non-striated cells
Has a voluntary and fast contraction
Never fatigues
Is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is striped/red, striated, attached to the skeleton, voluntary and fast, fatigues fast and is controlled by the CNS. Never fatiguing and ANS control belong to cardiac and visceral muscle.

options: Has a voluntary contraction
Has an involuntary, automatic, rhythmic and fast contraction
Is made of striated cells
Is located in the heart walls
Is also called mixed muscle
questions.explanation: In the lesson's table cardiac muscle = mixed: striated cells like skeletal muscle, but involuntary/automatic/rhythmic, never fatigues and is under ANS control.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the wall of a hollow viscus shows non-striated muscle cells. This muscle:
options: Is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
Contracts involuntarily, slowly and continuously
Fatigues fast
Is controlled by the central nervous system
Is visceral (smooth) muscle
questions.explanation: Visceral (smooth) muscle has non-striated cells, lines hollow viscera, vessel walls and skin, contracts involuntarily, slowly and continuously, never fatigues and is under ANS control.

questions.stem: About the situation of skeletal muscles:
options: Deep muscles are sub-aponeurotic
Facial muscles are deep muscles
Superficial muscles are supra-aponeurotic (subcutaneous)
Muscles attached to the digestive and respiratory systems are deep muscles
Muscles attached to the sensory organs are superficial muscles
questions.explanation: Two groups: deep (sub-aponeurotic: muscles of the digestive/respiratory systems, skeletal muscles, sensory organs) and superficial (supra-aponeurotic, subcutaneous: facial muscles).

options: Has tendons that are its contractile part
Has two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon
Has a belly that is large, red, fleshy and contractile
Has a middle muscular belly and two tendinous ends
Has tendons that are narrow, whitish, elastic and resistant
questions.explanation: The belly is the contractile part; tendons are the narrow whitish resistant ends. Two bellies with an intermediate tendon is a digastric muscle.

questions.stem: The biceps brachii and the quadriceps femoris:
options: The quadriceps femoris is a multigastric muscle
Their parallel tendons are called heads
Have intermediate tendons between successive bellies
Have bellies arranged in parallel
The biceps brachii is a bifid muscle
questions.explanation: Biceps = bifid (2 parallel bellies), quadriceps = multifidus (several parallel bellies); parallel tendons are called heads. Bellies in series with intermediate tendons define digastric/multigastric muscles.

questions.stem: A muscle has several bellies separated by several intermediate tendons:
options: The quadriceps femoris is an example
The digastric muscle is an example
It is a multigastric muscle
It is a multifidus muscle
The rectus abdominis is an example
questions.explanation: Several bellies + several intermediate tendons = multigastric (rectus abdominis). The digastric has only two bellies; the quadriceps is multifidus (parallel bellies).

options: The termination is distal or mobile
A muscle attaches by a double insertion: an origin and a termination
The origin is proximal or fixed
Insertion can occur on bone, cartilage, aponeurosis or skin
The origin always remains fixed
questions.explanation: Origin = proximal/fixed, termination = distal/mobile, but the origin can sometimes become mobile. The four insertion sites are bone, cartilage, aponeurosis and skin.

questions.stem: Which insertion type — example pairs are correct?
options: Bone insertion — iliopsoas muscle
Aponeurotic insertion — palmaris brevis muscle
Aponeurotic insertion — abductor hallucis muscle
Skin insertion — abductor hallucis muscle
Cartilage insertion — cricothyroid muscle
questions.explanation: Bone: iliopsoas; cartilage: cricothyroid; aponeurotic: abductor hallucis; skin: palmaris brevis.

options: A long muscle has its length predominating, e.g. sartorius
The trapezius is a long muscle
A short muscle has its three dimensions reduced, e.g. sartorius
Annular muscles surround openings, e.g. orbicularis oris
A flat muscle has length and width predominating over thickness, e.g. latissimus dorsi
questions.explanation: Long: sartorius; flat: latissimus dorsi; short: hypothenar muscles; annular: orbicularis oculi/oris; geometric: trapezius, pronator quadratus, depressor anguli oris.

questions.stem: During hand surgery, the surgeon opens a fibrous groove that, together with the bone, forms an osteofibrous canal in which the tendons slide. This structure is:
options: A fibrous sheath
A muscular fascia
A covering aponeurosis
A serous (synovial) bursa
A tendinous serous sheath
questions.explanation: Fibrous sheaths delimit an osteofibrous canal with the bone; inside it the tendons slide wrapped in tendinous serous sheaths. Fascia (covering aponeurosis) encases and separates muscles.

options: Muscular fascia is also called covering aponeurosis
Tendinous serous sheaths are fibrous grooves
There are four types of appendices
Muscular fascia is a membranous sac filled with synovial fluid
Serous bursae are sacs filled with synovial fluid that facilitate muscle gliding
questions.explanation: The four appendices: serous bursae (synovial-fluid sacs near joints), tendinous serous sheaths (bursae around tendons), fibrous sheaths (fibrous grooves) and muscular fascia (encases and separates muscles).
